headline: Scientists name a new wild cat. It weighs 3 pounds.
summary: The cat has lived for years at a wildlife sanctuary in Bolivia after a local family took it in. DNA from more than 30 cats, plus museum bones and skins, showed it is a species nobody had described. It is named Leopardus tilcayo, the name local communities already used. The last new wild cat species was named in 1923.

cover_question.q: How do you find a new kind of cat?

cover_answer: Check its DNA. This one hid in plain sight for years.
table_question: Should a new animal get a scientist's name, or the local one?

5-7.script: Scientists found a kind of wild cat nobody knew about. It lives at an animal rescue place in Bolivia, and it is smaller than a house cat: three pounds, about as heavy as a bag of apples. It has light brown fur with dark spots. Nobody knew it was special until scientists checked, and now it has a name and people looking after it.
5-7.why: A tiny spotted cat with a new name is a story a six-year-old can hold all of.

8-12.script: Someone in Bolivia found a spotted kitten in the forest and took it for a house cat. It grew up at a sanctuary, where a biologist thought it looked odd. Scientists checked its DNA against more than 30 other cats, like fingerprints. None matched, so it got its own name.
8-12.why: Notice, check, name is a chain they can follow.

13-17.script: Where does a new cat species turn up: the deep wild, or a rescue center? This one lived at a sanctuary in Bolivia before anyone tested its DNA. The study says it is one of at least five tiger cat species once counted as one. What else is filed under the wrong name?
13-17.why: Teens like it when the experts had it wrong. Let them run with it.

5-7.a: No. It's a wild cat, and only one has been found. It lives at a sanctuary in Bolivia where people look after it.

8-12.q: How do you find a new kind of cat?
8-12.a: Scientists compared its DNA with more than 30 other cats, plus museum bones and skins. It matched none.
Tiger cats all look alike, even to experts. This one sat at a sanctuary for years and nobody had checked.

13-17.q: How is it new if it looks like the others?
13-17.a: Its DNA. The study says its line split from its relatives about 1.4 million years ago. Looks can hide that.

13-17.q: What's the point of naming it?
13-17.a: Researchers say you can't protect what you haven't named. Its forest faces deforestation and mining.
